hints: Think about what makes the carbon in $\text{C-Br}$ attractive to a nucleophile, consider electronegativity difference and partial charges.
Remember a curly arrow always starts from an electron source such as a lone pair or a bond, and points to where those electrons go.
walkthrough:
Spot the electron rich and electron poor centres**
Picture $^{-}\text{CN}$ with its lone pair on carbon. That is your nucleophile, full of electrons looking for a positive centre. In bromoethane the Br pulls electrons away from carbon, so that carbon is $\delta+$ and Br is $\delta-$. Mark that dipole clearly.

Make the new bond and break the old bond**
Let the lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ flow to the $\delta+$ carbon with a curly arrow starting on the lone pair and pointing to the carbon. At the same time, the $\text{C-Br}$ bonding pair must leave with Br, so draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br. That gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}$ plus $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Final answer: Lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^{-}$ with curly arrow from lone pair to C of $\text{C-Br}$ ($\delta+$).
$\text{C-Br}$ shown as $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ with curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br to give $\text{Br}^{-}$.

hints: Look at what happens to the oxygen content when propanoic acid $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ becomes W using $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$.
walkthrough:
Recognise LiAlH4 as a reducer**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ is a powerful reducing agent that supplies hydride. Here $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ loses oxygen to form $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ (W). Loss of oxygen and gain of hydrogen means reduction.

hints: Recall the characteristic IR wavenumber ranges for a carboxylic acid $\text{C=O}$ and for an alcohol $\text{O-H}$.
Link the functional group change from $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ to which peak should vanish and which should appear or change.
walkthrough:
List what each molecule can absorb**
Propanoic acid has $\text{C=O}$ which gives a very strong sharp dip around $1700$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$. W is propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, which has no $\text{C=O}$ but has an alcohol $\text{O-H}$.

Predict the clear spectral change**
So you will lose the $\text{C=O}$ peak at $1680$ to $1730$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ when the acid is reduced. Alternatively you can describe the alcohol $\text{O-H}$ broad absorption at $3200$ to $3650$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ appearing in W. Either paired observation plus explanation earns full credit.
Final answer: Disappearance of absorption at 1680-1730 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to loss of $\text{C=O}$ OR appearance of absorption at 3200-3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to formation of alcohol $\text{O-H}$.

hints: Reaction 4 converts bromoethane to ethanol, decide whether $\text{Br}$ is replaced by $\text{OH}$ or removed to form a double bond.
Think about which solvent favours substitution by $\text{OH}^{-}$ rather than elimination.
walkthrough:
Identify substitution to an alcohol**
Going from $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ is replacement of Br by OH, so the reagent must supply $\text{OH}^{-}$. That is $\text{NaOH}$ or $\text{KOH}$.

Choose water to favour substitution**
Use aqueous conditions. Water as solvent favours nucleophilic substitution. Ethanolic conditions would push the reaction toward elimination instead.

Final answer: reagent: sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide
conditions: aqueous

hints: Reaction 5 converts bromoethane to ethene, so consider how the conditions must change to favour elimination over substitution with the same $\text{OH}^{-}$ reagent.
walkthrough:
Switch solvent to favour elimination**
The same $\text{OH}^{-}$ can act as a base to remove $\text{HBr}$ and form $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CH}_{2}$. Using ethanol as solvent, with heat, favours elimination (reaction 5) rather than substitution.
Final answer: ethanolic (heat)

hints: Recall what catalyst is needed for condensation between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol to form an ester plus water.
walkthrough:
Catalyse ester formation with strong acid**
Ethanol plus propanoic acid gives an ester by condensation with loss of water. This needs a concentrated strong acid catalyst, typically concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$, to protonate the carbonyl and remove water.
Final answer: concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ or concentrated $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ or concentrated $\text{H}^{+}$ / acid

hints: Join $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}-$ from the acid to $-\text{OCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ from the alcohol and sketch the carbon skeleton as lines.
walkthrough:
Build the ester linkage**
Take the acid part $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(=O)}-$ and attach $-\text{O}-\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ from ethanol. In skeletal form draw connected lines for $\text{C-C-C(=O)-O-C-C}$, showing the double bond $\text{C=O}$ clearly.
Final answer: Skeletal formula of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$: zigzag of 5 atoms with $\text{C=O}$ on central carbonyl carbon linked to O.

hints: Name an ester as alkyl alkanoate, with the alcohol part first and the acid part second.
walkthrough:
Apply alkyl alkanoate naming**
The $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}-$ from ethanol gives ethyl, and the $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COO}-$ from propanoic acid gives propanoate. Together this is ethyl propanoate.

hints: V decolourises bromine water so it is an alkene, and hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{H}^{+}$ cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ to give only propanoic acid, so think about what symmetrical alkene gives two identical 3 carbon acids.
Cold dilute $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{H}^{+}$ adds two $\text{OH}$ groups across the double bond without cleavage, so add $\text{OH}$ to each $\text{C=C}$ carbon of V to get T.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the cleavage product**
V must be an alkene because it decolourises bromine water. Hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{H}^{+}$ splits the $\text{C=C}$ completely. Getting only $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ as the organic product means both halves are identical 3 carbon fragments. Joining two $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C}$ units through a double bond gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH=CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$.

Form the mild oxidation product**
Cold dilute $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{H}^{+}$ does not cleave, it adds one $\text{OH}$ to each carbon of the double bond. Adding $\text{OH}$ to C3 and C4 of hex-3-ene gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, which indeed has two chiral centres at C3 and C4.

Final answer: V = $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH=CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ (hex-3-ene)
T = $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ (hexane-3,4-diol)

hints: For V, check whether each $\text{C=C}$ carbon has two different groups attached, allowing cis trans arrangements.
For T, use the information that it has two chiral centres with four different groups on carbon to decide the type of stereoisomerism.
walkthrough:
Assign V as geometric**
In $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH=CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ each double bond carbon carries H and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, two different groups. The double bond cannot rotate, so cis (Z) and trans (E) forms exist. That is geometric isomerism.

Assign T as optical**
In $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ carbons 3 and 4 each carry H, OH, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, four different groups. Carbons with four different groups are chiral and give non superimposable mirror images, which is optical isomerism.

Final answer: V: geometric (cis-trans / E-Z) isomerism
T: optical isomerism
